description: Rearmament, Four-Year Plan, Strength Through Joy — and the workers, women and farmers who paid for it.
content_html:
Economy, Society and Nazi Winners and Losers

The Nazi regime’s economic performance is one of the most contested areas of its history. Headline statistics look striking: unemployment fell from approximately six million in early 1933 to under 200,000 by 1939. But these numbers conceal as much as they reveal. Understanding who benefited from Nazi economic policy, and who paid for it, is essential to any balanced assessment.

Economic Recovery and Rearmament

Initial recovery owed something to policies already in train under Brüning and von Papen, and to the normal business cycle turning upward from the 1932 trough. But the Nazis accelerated recovery through massive state spending, particularly on rearmament and public works. The RAD (Reich Labour Service), established in 1933, removed young men from the unemployment register and put them to work on public projects. The new Autobahn network was presented as evidence of national renewal.

Economist Hjalmar Schacht’s “New Plan” of 1934 directed imports towards rearmament priorities and managed the foreign exchange crisis. From 1936 the Four-Year Plan under Hermann Göring took over, explicitly prioritising military production. Germany was to be war-ready by 1940. Schacht resigned in 1937, warning that the pace of rearmament was economically unsustainable — he was correct, but ignored.

Key Fact

Nazi unemployment statistics excluded women (many of whom were removed from the labour market by policy), Jewish workers, and those on compulsory RAD or military service. The real unemployment picture was more complex than the headline figures suggested.

Winners and Losers: Workers

Workers were in an ambiguous position. On one hand, the return of employment after the misery of the Depression was genuinely welcomed. The German Labour Front (Deutsche Arbeitsfront), led by Robert Ley, replaced independent trade unions (banned in May 1933) and provided leisure activities through the Strength Through Joy (Kraft durch Freude) programme, including subsidised holidays, concerts and even ocean cruises.

But workers lost the right to strike, lost independent trade unions, and saw real wages stagnate or decline as government spending on rearmament crowded out consumer goods. The Strength Through Joy holidays were real but accessible mainly to better-paid workers; many working-class families remained poor throughout the 1930s. The promise of a Volkswagen (“People’s Car”) through a savings scheme attracted 340,000 subscribers by 1939 — yet no civilian vehicle was ever delivered before the war began.

The Nazi ideal for women was encapsulated in the three Ks: Kinder, Küche, Kirche (Children, Kitchen, Church). Women were encouraged to leave paid employment, marry, and produce children for the Aryan nation. The Reich Mothers’ Cross, introduced in 1933, awarded medals to women for having four (bronze), six (silver) or eight or more (gold) children. Marriage loans were offered to couples on condition that the woman gave up work.

In reality, policy contradicted ideology. As rearmament accelerated and male labour was absorbed into the army, women were increasingly needed in factories and farms. By the late 1930s the regime was actively encouraging women to work again, despite its own propaganda. During the war years female employment rose dramatically. The “ideal” of the stay-at-home mother was always in tension with military-economic reality.

Youth and the Hitler Youth

Young people were a priority target for the regime. The Hitler Youth (Hitlerjugend) enrolled boys from age 14, with the younger Jungvolk for ages 10–14. Girls joined the League of German Girls (BDM — Bund Deutscher Mädel). Membership was made compulsory in 1936 and universal by 1939. The Hitler Youth combined outdoor activities, sport, camping and marching with ideological indoctrination. It was genuinely popular with many young Germans, offering excitement, community and a sense of purpose.

But the Hitler Youth also crowded out older youth organisations — church youth groups, sports clubs — and subjected young people to constant ideological pressure. Teachers who tried to resist found their authority undermined. Some young people rejected the organisation entirely, joining underground youth subcultures like the Edelweiss Pirates.

Key Fact

Three groups who lost under Nazi policy: workers (lost trade unions and collective bargaining, real wages stagnated); women (pressured to leave work, but later recalled for the war economy anyway); the Mittelstand (small business owners who gained initially from anti-department-store measures but were squeezed by the war economy).

Farmers had been among the earliest Nazi supporters, attracted by promises of agricultural protection. The Reich Entailed Farm Law of 1933 guaranteed peasant ownership of medium-sized farms from seizure for debt — a genuine protection. But agricultural prices remained relatively low, farm labour was drawn into better-paid industrial work, and the Four-Year Plan’s demand for food self-sufficiency placed heavy demands on farmers without adequate reward.

The Mittelstand (lower middle class) had been enthusiastic Nazi voters in 1930–32. The regime made some gestures — closing some Jewish department stores, protecting artisan trades — but the Four-Year Plan’s focus on heavy industry left small businesses at a disadvantage. The economic “miracle” benefited big business and armaments manufacturers far more than the independent small trader.
exam_tip_html: The “winners and losers” question is a classic exam topic. Avoid listing groups without analysis: examiners want you to explain the mechanisms by which each group gained or lost and to weigh these against each other. Remember to interrogate the unemployment statistics — showing you know they excluded women, Jewish workers and those on compulsory schemes demonstrates sophisticated contextual knowledge. The strongest answers also link social policy to the regime’s broader aims: rearmament, racial state, preparing for war.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Unemployment fell from 6 million to under 200,000 by 1939, but the statistics excluded women, Jews and those on compulsory schemes; the recovery was built on rearmament spending that prioritised guns over consumer goods.
  • Workers lost trade unions and collective bargaining rights; women were pressured out of work by ideology but recalled into it by economic necessity; farmers and the Mittelstand gained limited protections that were quickly undermined by war-economy priorities.
  • Strength Through Joy and the Hitler Youth offered genuine benefits to some, but were tools of social control as much as welfare, designed to build loyalty and distract from lost freedoms.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Four-Year Plan (1936).
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Precise feature with accurate detail (e.g. the Four-Year Plan, launched in 1936 under Hermann Göring, aimed to make Germany self-sufficient and war-ready by 1940 by prioritising military production over consumer goods). Secure: Valid feature with some detail. Developing: Relevant but vague. Emerging: Inaccurate.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Strength Through Joy programme.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two precise features (e.g. provided subsidised holidays, concerts, theatre and ocean cruises for German workers; run by the German Labour Front as a replacement for independent trade unions that had been banned). Secure: Two features with some detail. Developing: Two features without sufficient detail. Emerging: One vague point.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Nazi economic recovery of the 1930s was not as beneficial for German workers as the unemployment figures suggest.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses multiple reasons — unemployment statistics excluded women, Jews and those on compulsory schemes; real wages stagnant or falling; loss of trade unions and collective bargaining; consumer goods sacrificed for rearmament; Volkswagen savings scheme never delivered. Secure: Two or more reasons with relevant evidence. Developing: One reason with explanation. Emerging: Simple general points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the Nazi regime's social and economic policies created winners and losers within German society.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two well-developed points with precise evidence identifying who gained (big business, armaments producers, some farmers initially, Hitler Youth participants) and who lost (workers losing unions, women pressured out of work, Mittelstand squeezed by war economy, Jewish workers excluded). Secure: Two points with relevant evidence. Developing: Two points with limited analysis. Emerging: One point or vague.

practice_questions.text: How significant was rearmament in shaping the experiences of different groups within German society in the years 1933–1939?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Analyses rearmament's impact across multiple groups (workers losing real wages as consumer goods were sacrificed; big business gaining contracts; farmers pressured for food self-sufficiency; women recalled into workforce despite ideology) and assesses relative significance against other factors (propaganda, terror, social welfare initiatives). Secure: Considers rearmament's impact and compares with other factors. Developing: Describes rearmament without comparative analysis. Emerging: General and descriptive.

practice_questions.text: Assess the view that Nazi economic policy benefited most German people in the years 1933–1939. How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Balanced argument: genuine benefits (falling unemployment, Strength Through Joy, Hitler Youth, rearmament creating jobs) set against costs and limitations (loss of unions, manipulated statistics, real wage stagnation, policy failures for Mittelstand and farmers, Four-Year Plan's consumer sacrifice). Precise evidence; substantiated conclusion. Secure: Both sides with evidence. Developing: Unbalanced. Emerging: Descriptive.

glossary_terms.definition: Reich Labour Service — compulsory work scheme removing young men from the unemployment register and putting them to work on public projects such as roads and land drainage.
System of motorways built from 1933, used as both practical infrastructure and propaganda evidence of national renewal.
Reichsbank president and Economics Minister 1934–1937 whose 'New Plan' directed imports towards rearmament needs; resigned in 1937 over the pace of rearmament.
Economic programme launched in 1936 under Hermann Göring, aiming to make Germany self-sufficient and war-ready within four years by prioritising military production over consumer goods.
Organisation created in 1933 to replace independent trade unions, providing leisure activities but no collective bargaining rights, run by Robert Ley.
Leisure organisation for German workers run by the German Labour Front, providing subsidised holidays, concerts and sports activities to create loyalty.
The 'People's Car' — announced in 1938 as affordable through a savings scheme, but no civilian car was ever delivered before the war began.
Nazi youth organisation for boys aged 14–18 that became compulsory for all German youth by 1939, combining outdoor activities with ideological indoctrination.
The lower middle class of small business owners, shopkeepers and artisans — a key constituency of early Nazi support who were ultimately disadvantaged by the Four-Year Plan's priorities.
